drafts.label: Reply · thinking on your own should not be a luxury
drafts.body:
This line hits because it is almost true already.

We will make AI so cheap that only the rich will think on their own — unless education changes the incentive.

If the grade only rewards the polished last frame, outsourcing thinking is rational. Cheap answers + output-only assessment = cognitive offloading for everyone, not just the poor.

My take: make the scarce skill visible. Assess the path — what a student can defend without the model — and thinking on your own stops being a luxury brand.
drafts.why: Same-day high-signal one-liner on cheap AI vs owned thinking; 86 likes / ~10k views. Grounded only in his AI-so-cheap / think-on-their-own riff.
drafts.tip: Copy & open first. Soft process-assessment bridge only. Do not invent Edison biography or economics beyond the parallel he set up.

drafts.label: Reply · learning experiences not just answer videos
drafts.body:
This is the education use case I want more of.

Video models letting one person turn a vision into a learning experience that used to need a full production team — that is real access.

But the win is not only prettier content. It is when the media still forces the learner to notice, recall, and check themselves — not just watch a polished answer stream.

Student-centric means the path of understanding stays in the loop. Tools like this can scaffold that if we design for thinking, not only for the final clip.
drafts.why: Same-day AI-ed demo; 77 likes / solid bookmarks. Claims limited to video models revolutionize education + vision→prompt→learning experience once needing production team.
drafts.tip: Stay on education access + learning experience. Do not invent curriculum outcomes beyond what the post states. Soft process note only.

drafts.label: Short · cheap tools, scarce owned thinking
drafts.body:
AI is getting cheaper and better at producing learning media.

That does not automatically make people better thinkers. It makes polished answers cheaper.

The scarce skill is still owned thinking — the path you can defend without the model. Assess that, or cheap AI just scales cognitive offloading.

32 of 35 isnt a "students got lazier" story first. Its a measurement design story.

If the midterm only rewards a polished final sheet, AI becomes the rational path. Same with take-home averages jumping to 96% — the assessment is still scoring output, not how they reasoned.

Invisible traps catch the symptom. What actually changes behavior is assessing process, judgment, and what they can defend without the tool.

Otherwise we keep measuring the wrong thing and acting shocked at the score.
drafts.why: Hyper-fresh (~1h) viral education/AI cheating post; 290+ likes / 50+ replies / climbing. Grounded only in 32/35 + Brown take-home 96% claims from the post.
drafts.tip: Copy & open source first; do not invent method details beyond invisible prompt + numbers stated.

drafts.label: Reply · questions worth asking is the scarce skill
drafts.body:
Absolutely correct. The bottleneck shifted.

When AI can explain, write, and research in seconds, memorizing the answer is almost free. Judgement — which questions are worth asking — is the scarce skill.

Most education still scores the finished answer sheet. That trains people to outsource the thinking and polish the output.

If we want curiosity and creativity to compound, we have to assess the path of thinking, not only the last frame.
drafts.why: Fresh (~1–2h) India-visible education thesis; 140+ likes. Claims limited to AI speed vs human question-selection + teach thinking not memorize.
drafts.tip: Stay on judgment/curiosity; soft process bridge only — no product pitch dump.

drafts.label: Short · students optimize what we grade
drafts.body:
Cheating scandals keep proving the same thing.

Students are optimizing for what we grade. If we only grade the final submission, AI is the efficient move.

Change the goal of assessment — process, defense, the questions they choose — and the behavior of learning shifts with it.
drafts.why: Original Venn thesis for timeline; no fake citations.

I did. And I get why it feels like a flex.

But the useful question isnt only "did we survive without it" — its what cognitive habits we built because there was no answer machine.

The danger now is not that students have ChatGPT. Its that formal education still scores the final sheet the same way, so the easy path is offloading the thinking and polishing the output.

If we change what we measure — process, judgment, how they work with the tool — the brag becomes less about nostalgia and more about systems that still force deep thinking.

drafts.label: Reply · syllabus lag still needs process scores
drafts.body:
You're right — the syllabus lag is real. Businesses every few years, tech every few months, AI every few weeks… curriculum every few decades. We need to move.

But updating the chapter list alone wont close the gap. If we still only score the final answer sheet, students will just use AI to produce a prettier sheet for the same old goals.

My take: we need to move what we measure. Student-centric methods + process-based assessment — the thinking path, judgment, how they work with the tool — not only the last frame.

Change the goal of assessment and the behavior of learning will change with it.

drafts.label: Reply · cheaper access + training > lock-in
drafts.body:
You're absolutely right on the last point — and that's the part most debates skip.

If we actually care how people use AI, locking intelligence behind closed walls doesn't fix the cognitive problem. It just picks who gets to offload thinking.

Easier and cheaper access only helps when we also build the learning layer: training that forces reasoning, student-centric practice, assessment that scores the process — not a prettier final answer.

Open / efficient models are how that access scales beyond a few labs. Without the learning design, access is just faster answers.

drafts.tip: Copy & open source first; keep product soft or skip name if tight.

drafts.label: Reply · education past memorizing still needs process scores
drafts.body:
You're right that education has to move past memorizing answers toward creativity, judgment, and working with intelligent machines.

My take: if we still only score the final sheet, students will just use AI to produce a cleaner final sheet. The behavior doesn't change — the offloading just gets better at hiding.

The real shift is student-centric. Score the thinking path and the judgment in how they use the tool, not whether the last answer looks smart. Otherwise the "augmented vs unaugmented" divide becomes who can hide cognitive offloading better.
drafts.why: Fresh education+AI post; process assessment angle grounded in his claims.
drafts.tip: His frame is future-of-work — land on assessment without lecture tone.

drafts.label: Short · access without learning design
drafts.body:
AI access without learning design is just faster answers.

If we want people sharper, not lazier, we need both:
- open / cheap / fast models so more people can actually use serious AI
- education and assessment that reward the process of thinking

That's the intersection I'm building around.
